17) I like to see that insiders own a significant portion of the company. It’s not a must, but it’s clearly an advantage when insiders have skin in the game.
16) The market is usually slow to price in good and bad reports, which creates opportunities if you’re quick to react.

15) I avoid companies with large net debt, as it increases the risk in the case, and there’s a chance the company will have to raise new money through an equity issuance, leading to the risk of dilution.
14) If the valuation becomes too high based on my next-twelve-months estimates, I trim the position or sell entirely.

13) I usually have between 8–12 companies in my portfolio. This creates less volatility than having, say, 5–6 companies, and it gives me more flexibility to adjust weightings in my holdings depending on conviction and valuation.
12) If a company reports a very bad quarter, the next quarters are usually also bad. Therefore, it often proves to be a good idea to sell on bad reports/news.
as they can invest more in R&D, brand, and service than smaller competitors.

11) I prefer small niche companies that are market leaders in their small niche. Becoming a market leader can create advantages like pricing power, and it also makes it easier to widen the moat against competitors
10) I prefer companies that focus on organic growth, and possibly small bolt-on acquisitions that complement the core business. Companies driven by inorganic growth are often too risky.
In rare cases, I might invest in these if the upside versus risk looks very favorable.

9) I prefer companies that are not heavily affected by macroeconomic cycles. The reason is that I don’t have the competence to time those cycles, so I generally avoid investing in banks, oil companies, property developers, and mining companies.
I have positions that have grown to 30–35% of the portfolio because they have increased revenue and EBIT over many years, while the valuation hasn’t become too high.

8) “Let your winners run.” I believe more in averaging up in stocks than averaging down. When I find an attractive stock, I usually build a 3–10% position based on my conviction. If the company proves itself over time, I buy more.

7) I prefer simple business models that are easy to understand, preferably with recurring revenue or relatively predictable revenue. I generally avoid companies that fluctuate a lot from quarter to quarter in revenue, though there can be exceptions.

6) Investing in intelligent fanatics — meaning you should find CEOs with a proven track record who have demonstrated they can grow revenue and scale EBIT, who are trustworthy (i.e., the CEO delivers on what they promise), and who have that spark in their eye.
5) I like to invest in companies where I can find alternative data that gives me an edge over most other investors.

4) I don’t mind paying a relatively high multiple if the quality is sufficiently high. By quality, I mean companies with a strong track record, an excellent business model (e.g., SaaS), good future prospects, and strong moats.

3) The perfect cases are usually overlooked, misunderstood, and cheap. If the company increases revenue and scales EBIT over time, their multiple will rise because investors gain increased conviction, while at the same time you get increased EPS growth.
2) Focus on small companies, preferably before larger institutional investors get involved, as they are often "mispriced" due to very little attention on them.
1) Investing in profitable companies, or companies that are 1–2 quarters away from achieving profitability, because one of the worst things that can happen is getting diluted.
